Heat sensors on their noses help them find the warmest spots where blood flows close to the skin.

Musk oxen survive brutal Arctic winters thanks to a soft undercoat called qiviut, which is far warmer than sheep's wool for its weight. When threatened by wolves, the herd forms a defensive circle with horns facing out and the calves protected in the middle. They shed the warm underwool naturally in spring, and it can be gathered from bushes without harming the animal.

The tarsier is a tiny primate whose eyes are so huge that each eyeball is bigger than its brain and can't move in the socket. To make up for it, the tarsier can swivel its head around almost like an owl to look behind itself. Those giant eyes give it superb night vision for hunting insects in the dark.

When an opossum is terrified it can flop over and 'play dead' involuntarily, even drooling and giving off a rotten smell to convince predators it's a spoiled carcass. Opossums are also highly resistant to many snake venoms thanks to a special protein in their blood. Their low body temperature makes them very unlikely to carry rabies compared to other mammals.

Arctic ground squirrels can let parts of their body dip below the freezing point of water during hibernation, a state called supercooling, without forming damaging ice crystals. Their body temperature drops lower than any other known mammal while they hibernate. Every couple of weeks they briefly warm back up for a short rest before chilling down again.

The okapi looks like a mix of a horse and a zebra but is actually the giraffe's only close living relative. Its tongue is long enough to reach up and clean its own eyes and ears. The striped pattern on its rear helps calves follow their mother through the dim rainforest, and its big ears can swivel to catch the faintest sounds.

The aardvark is a champion digger, able to tunnel into a termite mound faster than several people with shovels using its powerful, claw-tipped feet. Its long sticky tongue can slurp up tens of thousands of insects in a single night. It can also seal its nostrils shut to keep biting insects and dust out while it feeds.

Manatees wear down their teeth by chewing gritty water plants all day, so they grow a constant supply of new teeth at the back that slowly march forward to replace the worn ones in front. This 'conveyor belt' of teeth keeps going their whole lives. They also have flexible, split upper lips that move almost like fingers to grab and pull plants into their mouths.

Reindeer can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to humans, helping them spot things in the snowy Arctic that would otherwise blend in, like lichen to eat or wolf fur. Part of their eye even changes color with the seasons, shifting toward blue in the long, dark winter to gather more light. Their wide hooves spread out like snowshoes and act as scoops for digging through snow.

Snow leopards live higher up the mountains than almost any other big cat, sometimes above 18,000 feet. Their tail is nearly as long as their body and packed with fat, so they wrap it around themselves like a scarf to stay warm. They can leap roughly 50 feet across a gully, one of the longest jumps of any cat.

Jaguars have the strongest bite of any big cat relative to their size, strong enough to crunch straight through a turtle's shell or pierce a skull. While most cats go for the throat, a jaguar often kills by biting directly through the back of the head. Its name comes from a Native word meaning roughly 'he who kills in one leap'.

Great white sharks can sense the tiny electric fields given off by a beating heart or twitching muscle, using jelly-filled pores around the snout called the ampullae of Lorenzini. This lets them detect prey buried in sand or hidden in murky water. The sense is so fine they can pick up signals far weaker than a flashlight battery would produce in the sea.

Spotted hyenas live in clans run entirely by females, and even the lowest-ranking female outranks the top male. They're not scavengers picking up lion leftovers, they're skilled pack hunters that lions frequently steal from instead. Their jaws are strong enough to crack and digest bone, so almost nothing of a carcass goes to waste.

The cougar holds a record for most names of any animal, known as puma, mountain lion, panther, catamount, and dozens more across the Americas. Despite its size it can't roar, because it belongs to the group of cats that purr instead. It can leap straight up about 18 feet, useful for ambushing prey from a ledge.

A golden eagle's grip is many times stronger than a human hand, and its talons can puncture deep into prey on impact. They've been recorded diving at speeds rivaling a falcon and have taken animals as large as young deer and goats. Their eyesight is sharp enough to spot a rabbit from over a mile away.

The clouded leopard has the longest canine teeth relative to skull size of any living cat, earning it the nickname 'modern saber-tooth'. Its ankles can rotate backward, letting it climb down trees headfirst and even hang from a branch by its back feet. This makes it one of the most acrobatic climbers in the entire cat family.

The wolverine looks like a small bear but is actually the largest member of the weasel family, and it punches far above its weight. It will drive bears and wolves off a kill and has special teeth that rotate to tear into meat frozen solid. A single wolverine may roam a territory the size of a small country in search of food.

Bald eagles are skilled fishers, but they're also opportunists that often steal catches from ospreys mid-air rather than do their own work. Benjamin Franklin famously grumbled about this, calling the eagle a bird 'of bad moral character'. Their nests are among the largest of any bird, sometimes weighing as much as a small car after years of additions.

African wild dogs are among the most successful hunters on land, catching prey on a large share of their chases, far better than lions. Before setting off to hunt, the pack 'votes' with a round of sneezes, and more sneezes mean the group is more likely to go. They share food generously, and pups are allowed to eat first at a kill.

The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world, with big females weighing more than a refrigerator. It kills not by crushing bones but by squeezing tighter each time prey breathes out, until the animal can't breathe in again. Anacondas spend most of their time in water, where their great weight is easier to move.

The black tufts on a lynx's ears aren't just decoration, they likely work like antennas that help funnel sound so the cat can pinpoint prey. Its huge furry feet act like built-in snowshoes, spreading its weight so it can chase hares across deep snow without sinking. A lynx's hearing is sharp enough to detect a mouse moving under the snowpack.

The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world, able to raise a third of its body straight up to look a person in the eye. It mainly eats other snakes, including other cobras. Unusually for a snake, the female builds a nest of leaves for her eggs and guards it fiercely until they're ready to hatch.

Smilodon, the famous saber-toothed cat, was built more like a wrestler than a runner, with a powerful front half for pinning prey rather than chasing it down. Its iconic fangs were long but surprisingly fragile and likely used for a precise killing bite once the prey was already held still. Many fossils come from tar pits where the cats got stuck trying to grab trapped animals.

The harpy eagle of South American rainforests has talons as large as a grizzly bear's claws, the better to snatch monkeys and sloths right out of the treetops. Despite this power, it's a quiet hunter that perches and waits, then drops on prey with little warning. Its wings are short and broad so it can weave between branches in dense forest.

The caracal is a desert cat famous for its sky-high leaps, able to spring several feet straight up to swat birds out of the air mid-flight. It can knock down more than one bird in a single jump. Its long black ear tufts twitch as it listens, and it can rotate each ear independently to track the faintest rustle.

In many crocodiles, including the Nile crocodile, whether a baby is male or female isn't set by genes but by the temperature of the nest while the eggs develop. Warmer and cooler nests tend to produce different sexes. The mother listens for chirps from inside the eggs, then gently carries the hatchlings to water in her giant mouth.

The great barracuda is a lightning-fast ambush hunter that can burst forward in short sprints to slash prey with its mouthful of dagger-like teeth. Its silvery body acts like a mirror underwater, helping it disappear against the shimmering surface until the final strike. Some teeth point backward so a struggling fish only works itself deeper into the jaws.

Madagascar's top predator is the fossa, a sleek cat-like hunter that's actually more closely related to the mongoose. It's one of the few predators agile enough to chase lemurs through the treetops, helped by a long tail for balance and ankles that swivel for headfirst descents. For its size it has an unusually large reach as a hunter, taking prey of many kinds.

The dhole, or Asiatic wild dog, hunts in packs that communicate with eerie whistles, which is why it's sometimes called the whistling dog. Working together, a pack can bring down prey many times the size of a single dhole and has even been recorded standing up to tigers. They're powerful jumpers and strong swimmers, sometimes driving prey into water to corner it.

The Tasmanian devil is the world's largest meat-eating marsupial and has one of the strongest bites for its size of any mammal, enough to crush bone. Early settlers named it 'devil' because of the bloodcurdling screeches it makes when squabbling over a carcass. It's a tireless scavenger that eats nearly every part of its food, fur and bones included.

Many bird bones are hollow, with internal struts that brace them like the cross-beams inside a bridge. This makes the skeleton light without making it weak. In some large soaring birds, the skeleton actually weighs less than all the feathers on the body.

Birds don't breathe in and out the way we do. Air flows through their lungs in one direction, looping through a system of air sacs so that fresh air passes over the lungs even while exhaling. This super-efficient setup helps birds get enough oxygen to fly hard at altitudes where humans would gasp.

Bar-headed geese migrate straight over the Himalayas, flying at heights where the air holds only a fraction of the oxygen we breathe at sea level. Their blood and muscles are specially tuned to grab oxygen efficiently. They've been recorded crossing some of the tallest mountains on Earth.

Hummingbirds are the only birds that can truly hover in place and even fly backward. They do it by sweeping their wings in a fast figure-eight pattern that makes lift on both the forward and backward stroke. Their wings can beat dozens of times every second, which is what makes the humming sound.

The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird and can glide for hours barely flapping. It uses a trick called dynamic soaring, stealing energy from the difference in wind speed at different heights above the waves. This lets it travel huge distances over the ocean while spending very little muscle energy.

Penguins can't fly through the air, but they basically fly through water. Their stiff, flipper-like wings flap the way other birds' wings beat the sky, pushing them through the sea at surprising speed. Their solid, heavy bones, the opposite of most birds, help them dive deep instead of floating.

Owls fly almost silently thanks to the edges of their wing feathers. The leading edge has a comb-like fringe and the trailing edge is soft and frayed, which breaks up the air and muffles the whoosh of flapping. This lets an owl swoop down on a mouse before the mouse ever hears it coming.

Many migrating birds can sense Earth's magnetic field and use it like a built-in compass. Some scientists think the ability lives in the bird's eyes, tied to special proteins that react to magnetism in faint light. Birds also read the position of the Sun and stars to find their way.

When geese fly in a V, each bird rides in the rising swirl of air left by the wingtip of the bird ahead, which saves energy. The leader works hardest, so birds take turns swapping out of the front position. Studies show they even time their wingbeats to catch the best lift.

Birds see colors we can't even imagine. Many have a fourth type of color receptor that picks up ultraviolet light, so feathers, flowers, and prey trails can glow in shades invisible to us. To a bird, a plain-looking meadow may be splashed with secret colors.

A bird's wing shape tells you how it lives. Short rounded wings let forest birds dart and turn through branches, long pointed wings suit fast flyers like swifts, and broad wings with splayed feather tips help eagles and vultures ride warm rising air. The shape is a clue to whether a bird sprints, cruises, or soars.

Hawks, vultures, and eagles often circle without flapping because they're riding thermals, columns of warm air rising off sunlit ground. The bird spirals upward inside the warm column for free, then glides off to find the next one. Migrating raptors string these thermals together to cover long distances on almost no effort.

A wing creates lift because it bends the air flowing over it downward, and the air pushes back up on the wing in return. The curved top and angled tilt help steer the air the right way. A bird constantly changes the angle and curve of its wings, something an airplane can only do in limited ways.

Feathers wear out, so birds replace them in a careful process called molting, usually a few at a time so the bird can keep flying. Some ducks and geese molt all their flight feathers at once and are grounded for weeks until new ones grow in. They often hide in safe spots until they can fly again.

A bird's tail acts as a brake, rudder, and extra wing all in one. By spreading or twisting it, a bird can slow down for landing, turn sharply, or add lift at slow speeds. Watch a pigeon land and you'll see the tail fan out wide at the last second.

Great frigatebirds can stay in the air for weeks over the open ocean without landing. They even sleep while flying, taking quick naps with one half of the brain at a time, often while gliding in a slow circle. They almost never touch the water because their feathers aren't waterproof.

Most birds launch into flight with a powerful jump from their legs, not by flapping from a standstill. That leap gives them the first burst of speed and height so the wings have moving air to work with. Heavy water birds like swans often need a long running start across the water to get going.

The kiwi of New Zealand has wings so tiny they're hidden under its shaggy feathers and useless for flight. Living for ages on islands with no big ground predators, its ancestors simply stopped needing to fly. Its feathers are soft and hair-like rather than the stiff, smooth kind built for the air.

Flying burns enormous energy, so birds run hot, fast engines. A small bird's heart can beat many hundreds of times a minute, and tiny birds must eat almost constantly to keep up. Their body temperature is usually warmer than ours, which helps their muscles fire quickly.

The bar-tailed godwit holds the record for the longest known nonstop flight, crossing the Pacific from Alaska to New Zealand in one go. It flies for more than a week without eating, drinking, or resting. Before it leaves, it fattens up and even shrinks some of its inner organs to save weight.

Many birds have an oil gland near the base of the tail that they nibble and spread across their feathers while preening. The oil helps keep feathers flexible and waterproof, which is why a duck can dive and come up nearly dry. A bird that can't preen properly soon gets waterlogged and cold.

Some birds, like chickadees and nutcrackers, hide thousands of seeds in different spots and remember where most of them are months later. The part of their brain used for memory actually grows larger in autumn when they need it most. They can outscore many mammals at remembering hidden locations.

The big burst of birdsong at sunrise, called the dawn chorus, happens partly because the cool, still morning air carries sound farther. Songs are mainly males announcing their territory and trying to attract mates. Many young birds have to learn their song by listening to adults, the way kids learn to talk.

Birds don't sing with a voice box like ours. They use a special organ called the syrinx, located deep in the chest where the windpipe splits toward the lungs. Because it has two sides that can work independently, some birds can sing two different notes at the same time.

A woodpecker hammers its beak into wood thousands of times a day at high speed, yet it doesn't get hurt. Its skull is built with spongy bone and a tongue that wraps around the back of the head, which together help absorb and spread the shock. Its brain is also packed snugly so it can't slosh around.

Because hummingbirds burn energy so fast, they can starve overnight while sleeping. To survive, they drop into a deep sleep-like state called torpor, slowing their heart and cooling their body to save fuel. In the morning it can take a while to warm back up before they can fly off to feed.

Homing pigeons can be carried hundreds of miles to an unfamiliar place and still find their way back to their loft. They seem to combine several tools, using the Sun, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, and even their sense of smell. For thousands of years people used them to carry messages across long distances.

Caddisfly larvae build tiny protective cases around their bodies using silk and whatever's lying on the streambed: sand grains, pebbles, leaf bits or snail shells. Each species favors its own building style, almost like an underwater signature. Clean-water artists have even fed them gold flakes and gemstones to make jewelry.

African lungfish can breathe air and survive a dried-up riverbed by burrowing into mud and wrapping themselves in a cocoon of hardened mucus. In this sleep-like state, called estivation, they can wait out months or even years of drought. When the rains return and the water rises, they wriggle free and swim off.

Mangroves are trees that grow with their feet in salty, oxygen-poor mud where most plants would die. Some pump excess salt out through their leaves, while others have roots that snorkel up into the air to grab oxygen. Their tangled roots shelter young fish and shield coastlines from storm waves.

The Amazon river dolphin, or boto, often turns pink as it ages and can twist its flexible neck to peer around flooded forest trunks. With tiny eyes nearly useless in muddy water, it relies on clicks and echoes to find fish. Its unfused neck vertebrae let it bend and maneuver between submerged branches.

Mayflies live underwater as nymphs for up to a year or two, but the winged adults often survive only a day or even just hours, just long enough to mate. They don't even have working mouths as adults. On some rivers, billions emerge at once in clouds so dense they show up on weather radar.

The Florida Everglades is often called a 'river of grass' because it really is a river, just an extraordinarily wide and shallow one creeping across the land. The water moves so slowly it can take months to drift from the middle of Florida down to the sea. Sawgrass, alligators and wading birds all depend on this sheet of moving water.

Hippos spend their days lounging in rivers because their thin skin dries out and burns in the sun. They produce a reddish oily secretion sometimes called 'blood sweat' that works as both sunscreen and an antibiotic. Despite being plant-eaters, hippos are among the most dangerous large animals in Africa.

The freshwater pearl mussel is one of the longest-living animals known, with some individuals surviving well over a century. Each one filters many liters of water a day, helping keep rivers clean. Their young hitch a ride by clamping onto the gills of young trout or salmon before dropping off to settle in the gravel.

Flamingos are born grey and turn pink only because of pigments in the tiny shrimp and algae they eat. Many gather on harsh, caustic soda lakes that few other animals can tolerate, feeding head-down with their bills upside-down to strain food from the water. A flamingo fed a different diet would slowly fade back toward white.

Water lilies and lotuses root in the muddy bottom and send long stems up to float their leaves on the surface, soaking up sunlight other underwater plants can't reach. Lotus leaves are so water-repellent that drops bead up and roll off, carrying away dirt. The giant Amazon water lily grows pads strong enough to hold the weight of a small child.

Peat bogs are wetlands so acidic and short on oxygen that dead plants barely rot, piling up over thousands of years into thick layers of peat. Because nothing decays properly, bogs have preserved ancient items perfectly, from butter to entire human bodies thousands of years old. Despite covering little land, the world's peatlands store a huge amount of carbon.

Sturgeon are living fossils, swimming the rivers and lakes in much the same shape as they had alongside the dinosaurs. Instead of normal scales they wear rows of bony plates called scutes, and they hoover up food from the bottom with whisker-like barbels. Some grow enormous and can live for over a century.

The North American Great Lakes hold about a fifth of the world's surface freshwater, carved out by glaciers grinding across the land during the last ice age. Lake Superior alone is so vast it could flood all of North and South America with water about a foot deep. Their shorelines stretch farther than the entire Atlantic coast of the United States.

River otters have some of the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs packed into a single square inch, trapping air to keep them warm without blubber. They're famously playful, sliding down muddy or snowy banks again and again seemingly just for fun. That play helps young otters build the swimming and hunting skills they'll need.

The capybara is the world's largest rodent, roughly the size of a big dog, and it lives a half-water life in the wetlands of South America. Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head so it can stay mostly submerged while still seeing, hearing and breathing. It can hold its breath and even nap underwater with just its nose poking out.

Most of the planet's liquid freshwater isn't in lakes or rivers at all but hidden underground, soaking the spaces between rocks and sand in layers called aquifers. This groundwater can be thousands of years old, having seeped down slowly over ages. Where it naturally bubbles back to the surface, it forms springs that feed many rivers and wetlands.

Leeches feed on blood using a clever trick: their saliva contains a chemical that stops blood from clotting, so a wound keeps flowing while they drink. That same chemical makes them useful in modern medicine, where doctors sometimes use leeches to keep blood moving in reattached fingers or skin grafts. Most leech species, though, eat tiny creatures rather than blood at all.

The kingfisher plunges headfirst into the water to snatch fish, and it can switch between seeing clearly in air and underwater by adjusting its eyes. It even has a special part of the eye that helps it correct for the way water bends light. To swallow a fish safely, it whacks the catch against a branch first so the spines fold flat.

Leafcutter ants don't actually eat the leaves they carry. They chew the leaves into a pulp and use it to grow a special fungus in underground gardens, and the fungus is what feeds the colony. They've been farming this way for tens of millions of years, long before humans figured out agriculture.

Dung beetles roll their ball of dung in a perfectly straight line to escape competitors at the pile. To stay straight on moonless nights, they steer by the glow of the Milky Way, making them the only animal known to navigate using the galaxy itself. They'll even climb on top of their ball to take a quick 'snapshot' of the sky before setting off.

The antlion larva digs a steep cone-shaped pit in loose sand and buries itself at the bottom with only its jaws exposed. When an ant slips over the edge, the larva flicks sand to start tiny landslides that drag the prey down. Adult antlions look like delicate, lacy-winged insects, completely unlike their fierce buried young.

The bombardier beetle defends itself by mixing two chemicals in a special internal chamber, producing a near-boiling spray it shoots from its rear end. The reaction happens in rapid pulses, like a tiny machine gun, and the beetle can aim the burning jet in almost any direction. Predators that get a faceful rarely come back for seconds.

Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground as nymphs before emerging all at once in enormous numbers. Both 13 and 17 are prime numbers, which scientists think makes it harder for predators with shorter life cycles to sync up with the swarm. When billions emerge together, predators simply can't eat them all, so plenty survive to breed.

A praying mantis can swivel its head nearly all the way around to track prey, something most insects can't do. It strikes out with its spiked front legs faster than the human eye can follow, snapping shut to pin a bug in place. Some of the largest mantises will even tackle small lizards, frogs, and hummingbirds.

Each firefly species flashes its own pattern of light to find a mate, like a flashing password in the dark. Females of one group, nicknamed femme fatale fireflies, mimic the flash code of other species to lure in hopeful males, then eat them. The light itself is almost perfectly efficient, producing a cool glow with very little wasted heat.

Aphids drink so much plant sap that they excrete sugary droplets called honeydew. Many ants 'herd' aphids like tiny cattle, stroking them with their antennae to milk the honeydew and protecting them from predators in return. Some ants even carry aphids to fresh plants and shelter their eggs over winter.

Weaver ants build nests by pulling living leaves together, with rows of workers forming chains to tug edges into place. To glue the leaves, other workers carry their own larvae and gently squeeze them so the young produce silk, using the babies like tubes of living glue. The whole colony cooperates on a single woven shelter high in the trees.

In honeypot ant colonies, certain workers act as living storage jars. They gorge on nectar and food until their bellies swell up like translucent grapes, then hang from the ceiling of the nest. When food is scarce, hungry nestmates tap them and they cough up a meal.

A cockroach can survive for a week or more without its head because it doesn't breathe through its mouth and its blood isn't pumped through narrow vessels under pressure. It breathes through tiny holes along its body and only dies because it eventually can't drink water. This toughness, plus eating almost anything, helps roaches thrive in many environments.

Dragonflies are among the most successful hunters in the animal world, catching the great majority of the prey they chase. Instead of simply following a target, a dragonfly predicts where the prey is going and flies to an interception point, like a skilled outfielder. Each of its four wings can move independently, letting it hover, fly backward, and turn on a dime.

When a giant hornet scout invades certain honeybee hives, hundreds of bees swarm over it in a tight ball and vibrate their flight muscles. This raises the temperature inside the ball just enough to cook the hornet to death while staying below the temperature the bees themselves can survive. It's defense by carefully controlled overheating.

Some assassin bugs that hunt ants pile the drained bodies of their victims onto their own backs, held in place with sticky secretions. This grisly backpack acts as both a disguise and possibly a shield, confusing other ants that rely on smell. Predators may also see a lump of debris rather than a vulnerable bug.

Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar doesn't just sprout wings; much of its body breaks down into a soupy mush. Small clusters of cells called imaginal discs, present since before pupation, rebuild that material into the adult butterfly's wings, legs, and eyes. Remarkably, experiments suggest some memories from the caterpillar stage can survive the rebuild.

Worker bees and queen bees can hatch from identical eggs; what makes a queen is her diet. Larvae chosen to become queens are fed only royal jelly, a protein-rich secretion, which switches on the genes for a larger body and working ovaries. Diet alone can turn an ordinary larva into the colony's egg-laying mother.

When floods hit, fire ants link their bodies together with jaws and legs to build a living raft that can float for days. The raft traps a layer of air so even the ants on the bottom can breathe, and they rotate positions so no one drowns. The whole colony, including the queen and brood, can ride out the water as one buoyant mass.

An ordinary solitary grasshopper can transform into a swarming locust when crowding triggers chemical changes in its body. As individuals bump into each other repeatedly, a surge of the brain chemical serotonin flips a switch, changing their color, behavior, and urge to gather. Millions then band together into swarms that can strip fields bare.

Stick insects don't just look like twigs; many gently sway as they walk to imitate a branch moving in the breeze. Some species can regrow a lost leg when they molt, and certain females can produce young without ever mating. A few even lay eggs that look exactly like plant seeds, complete with a coating that ants carry underground.

Many moths can hear the ultrasonic hunting calls of bats, which are too high-pitched for human ears. When a moth detects a distant bat, it flies away; when the bat is close, the moth may fold its wings and drop straight out of the sky to escape. Some tiger moths even click back to jam the bat's sonar or warn that they taste bad.

Bees see ultraviolet light that humans can't, which reveals hidden patterns on flowers. Many blooms have UV 'landing strips' that point straight to the nectar, invisible to us but glowing like runway lights to a bee. Flowers and their pollinators essentially evolved a secret signaling code we only discovered with special cameras.

Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need the protein in blood to develop their eggs; males sip flower nectar instead. Females track us by sensing the carbon dioxide in our breath from a distance, then home in using body heat, sweat odors, and even skin temperature. This layered set of senses makes them frustratingly good at finding a meal.

Tiny bugs called springtails, including the 'snow flea,' stay active in freezing weather by making their own antifreeze proteins. These proteins latch onto ice crystals and stop them from growing big enough to damage the body. You can spot snow fleas as specks of 'pepper' hopping on the surface of winter snow.

Honeybees build their comb out of six-sided wax cells, and hexagons happen to be the most efficient shape for storing the most honey with the least wax. Bees actually start by making round cells, and the heat and pressure from neighboring cells helps them settle into neat hexagons. The result is a lightweight, super-strong structure engineers still admire.

Beetles are the most diverse group of animals on Earth, with hundreds of thousands of named species and likely many more undiscovered. Roughly one in every four or five known animal species is a beetle, from speck-sized ones to palm-sized giants. When asked what could be learned about a creator from nature, one famous scientist supposedly quipped, 'an inordinate fondness for beetles.'

The young froghopper, or spittlebug, hides inside a frothy blob of bubbles often called cuckoo spit on plant stems. It makes the foam by mixing air with fluid pumped from its rear end, and the bubbles hide it from predators while keeping it from drying out. As an adult, the froghopper can jump higher relative to its size than almost any other animal.

Saharan desert ants find their way home across blank, scorching sand partly by counting their own steps, like a built-in pedometer. In a clever experiment, scientists glued tiny stilts onto some ants' legs so they took longer strides, and those ants overshot the nest, while ants with shortened legs stopped short. This showed the ants really do keep a running tally of how far they've walked.

Horseshoe crabs have blue blood because it carries copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin. Their blood is so good at detecting bacterial contamination that the medical industry harvests it to test vaccines and injectable drugs for safety. Despite the name, they are not crabs at all and are more closely related to spiders and scorpions.

Scorpions glow a bright blue-green under ultraviolet light because their hard outer shell contains fluorescent chemicals. Researchers think the whole body may act like a giant light sensor, helping the scorpion judge how dark its surroundings are so it knows when to hide. The glow even survives in fossils and in scorpions that have been preserved for decades.

The diving bell spider spends almost its whole life underwater, even though it still breathes air like other spiders. It spins a dome of silk and fills it with air bubbles carried down from the surface on its body hairs, creating an underwater air tank it can live, eat, and raise young inside. The silk dome even pulls oxygen out of the surrounding water like a gill.

House dust mites are microscopic arthropods that live in bedding, carpets, and furniture, feeding mostly on the tiny flakes of dead skin people shed every day. They are too small to see, yet a single used mattress can host hundreds of thousands of them. Most dust allergies are actually reactions to proteins in the mites' waste pellets rather than to the dust itself.

Spiders and other arthropods grow by climbing out of their old shell in a process called molting, because their hard outer skeleton cannot stretch. A molting spider becomes soft and helpless for a while until the new shell hardens, which is when it is most vulnerable. Some spiders can even regrow a missing leg over the next few molts.

The pill bug, or roly-poly, that lives under flowerpots is a land crustacean, far more closely related to crabs and shrimp than to insects. It breathes through gill-like structures that must stay moist, which is why it hides in damp places. Some species can roll into a tight armored ball, and certain ones carry copper in their blood the way horseshoe crabs do.

The coconut crab is the largest land-living arthropod, with a leg span that can reach about a meter across. It has claws strong enough to crack open coconuts and lift heavy objects, and adults actually drown if kept underwater because they breathe air. They climb trees and can live for decades.

Many spiders breathe using book lungs, organs filled with thin, stacked plates that look like the pages of a book and let oxygen seep into the blood. Air flows between the pages while blood flows inside them, so the spider can absorb oxygen without ever needing to actively pump air. Some spiders use these alongside or instead of breathing tubes called tracheae.

The smallest known insects are fairyflies, tiny parasitic wasps that are smaller than a grain of salt. Some species are smaller than a single-celled organism like an amoeba, and they spend much of their lives inside the eggs of other insects. To get airborne at that size, their wings are bristly fringed paddles rather than smooth blades.

Spiders that climb smooth walls and walk on ceilings do it with feet covered in thousands of microscopic hairs that split into even tinier tips. These tips get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the spider in place. The same trick lets a spider grip glass without any sticky glue at all.

Antarctic krill are small shrimp-like crustaceans that gather in swarms so enormous they can be seen from space and turn the sea red. Together they make up one of the largest amounts of any single animal on Earth by total weight. Whales, seals, penguins, and fish all depend on them, so this tiny creature helps hold up an entire ocean food web.

Trapdoor spiders build a silk-lined burrow capped with a camouflaged lid on a silk hinge, then wait underneath holding it shut. When a passing insect trips the silk trip-lines around the entrance, the spider flings the door open and grabs the prey in a fraction of a second. Some individual trapdoor spiders have been recorded living and guarding the same burrow for over forty years.

An orb-weaver spider lays down dry spokes first, then walks a spiral of sticky capture thread on top of them, and only the spiral is glued. That is why the spider can run across its own web without getting stuck: it knows to step only on the dry lines. Many of these spiders eat and rebuild the entire web every day to keep it fresh and sticky.

Despite their names, no centipede has exactly a hundred legs and no millipede has a thousand. Centipedes have one pair of legs per body segment and are fast venomous hunters, while millipedes have two pairs per segment and slowly graze on decaying leaves. One newly discovered millipede species did finally break the thousand-leg mark with over thirteen hundred.

Male fiddler crabs have one normal claw and one massively oversized claw that can make up a big share of their body weight, which they wave to attract mates and warn rivals. If a male loses the giant claw, the small claw can grow into a new large one, so the big claw can end up on either side. Despite its size, the huge claw is mostly for show and is fairly weak.

Young spiders travel huge distances by ballooning: they climb to a high point, raise their abdomens, and release strands of silk that lift them into the air. They can ride the wind for many miles and even cross oceans, sometimes landing on ships far from land. Earth's natural electric field in the atmosphere may give the silk an extra push to get airborne.

Hermit crabs have soft, unprotected back ends, so they live inside empty snail shells and must trade up to bigger ones as they grow. When a new larger shell appears, crabs sometimes line up by size and form a chain, each one stepping into the shell left behind by the next-bigger neighbor. That orderly handoff means a single empty shell can rehome a whole queue of crabs at once.

Spiders cannot eat solid food, so they pump digestive juices into or onto their prey and let it dissolve into a liquid first. Then they suck up the resulting soup, often leaving behind a hollow, drained shell of the insect. This is why a spider can never bite a chunk out of something larger than itself the way a mammal would.

Many tarantulas defend themselves by kicking clouds of tiny barbed hairs off their abdomens at attackers. These urticating hairs are intensely itchy and irritating to skin, eyes, and the noses of would-be predators. A tarantula can fling them so often that it leaves a visible bald patch on its own back.

Barnacles are crustaceans, not shellfish, and they spend their adult lives glued head-down to rocks, ships, and even whales. The natural cement they produce to cling on is one of the strongest known glues, holding firm underwater where ordinary adhesives fail. As larvae they swim freely, then pick a spot, stand on their heads, and never move again.

A spider on its web reads the world through vibrations, plucking and tightening the silk like guitar strings to judge the size and location of whatever lands on it. By the rhythm of the trembling it can tell the difference between a meal, a falling leaf, and an approaching mate. Some spiders even strum the threads to send signals back.

Camel spiders, also called wind scorpions or solifugids, are neither true spiders nor scorpions, but a separate group of arachnids. They have proportionally enormous jaws and are very fast runners across the desert, which fueled wild exaggerated stories among soldiers. In reality they are not venomous and are far smaller than the rumors claim.

When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance, walking in a figure-eight while shaking its body. The angle of the waggle relative to straight up tells the others the direction toward the food compared to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells them how far to fly. It is one of the only known cases of an animal giving symbolic directions.

The wood frog can survive being frozen nearly solid through the winter. Its heart stops beating, its blood stops flowing, and ice fills the spaces around its organs, while sugars and urea act like antifreeze to protect the cells themselves. When spring arrives it thaws out and hops away as if nothing happened.

The tuatara of New Zealand looks like a lizard but belongs to its own ancient order whose relatives mostly died out around the time of the dinosaurs. Young tuataras have a light-sensitive 'third eye' on the top of the head, complete with a lens and retina, that becomes covered by scales as they age. They can keep growing slowly for decades and may live well past 100 years.

The basilisk lizard can sprint across the surface of a pond on its hind legs, earning it the nickname 'Jesus Christ lizard.' It slaps its wide-toed feet down so fast that it traps a pocket of air and pushes off the water before it can sink. Young, lightweight basilisks can cross many feet of open water this way to escape predators.

Some horned lizards can shoot a stream of their own blood out of their eyes when threatened, sometimes a few feet. The blood contains chemicals that taste foul to dogs, coyotes, and other members of the dog family, often making them drop the lizard at once. The lizard does this by raising the blood pressure around its eyes until small vessels burst.

Caecilians are limbless amphibians that look like big earthworms or snakes and spend most of their lives burrowing underground or in streams. In several species the young feed by scraping off and eating their mother's outer skin, which she grows extra-thick and rich for them. They sense the world partly through a pair of small retractable tentacles on the face.

The leatherback is the largest turtle alive and, unlike other sea turtles, has no hard bony shell, just a leathery, ridged back over a layer of tough tissue. It can grow heavier than a small car and dive deeper than most whales while hunting jellyfish. Backward-pointing spines line its throat so slippery jellyfish cannot escape once swallowed.

Glass frogs of Central and South America have skin on their bellies so clear that you can see their heart, liver, and intestines through it. When they sleep on leaves by day, they pull most of their red blood cells into their liver, making their bodies far more transparent and harder for predators to spot. Hiding their blood this way is a clever trick that doesn't seem to harm them.

Geckos can run up glass and hang from a ceiling by one toe thanks to millions of tiny hairs on their feet called setae. These hairs are so fine that they cling to surfaces using a faint molecular attraction known as van der Waals forces, not glue or suction. A gecko peels each toe off in a curling motion so the grip releases cleanly with every step.

The alligator snapping turtle hunts by lying still on the riverbed with its mouth wide open, wiggling a pink, worm-shaped lure on its tongue. Fish swim in to grab the 'worm' and the turtle's jaws snap shut on them instead. These freshwater turtles can grow very heavy and live for many decades.

Pit vipers like rattlesnakes have heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils that detect the body warmth of nearby prey. The pits are sensitive enough to pick up tiny temperature differences, letting the snake 'see' a warm mouse in total darkness. The snake's brain blends this heat picture with its normal eyesight to aim a strike.

The hellbender is a giant salamander of North American rivers that can grow longer than your arm and breathes mostly through wrinkly folds of skin. Those baggy skin flaps add surface area so it can absorb oxygen straight from clean, cold, fast-flowing water. Because it needs such pure water, the presence of hellbenders is a sign that a stream is healthy.

The Surinam toad has one of the strangest ways of raising young in the animal world. The female's back swells over her eggs until they sink into pockets in her skin, where the babies develop in safety. Weeks later, fully formed little toads pop out of her back to start life on their own.

The thorny devil, a spiky desert lizard from Australia, can drink with its feet and skin instead of its mouth. Tiny grooves between its scales pull water by capillary action from damp sand or dew and channel it all the way to its mouth. This lets it stay hydrated in dry country where standing water is rare.

Some tree snakes in Southeast Asia can glide between branches and trees, flattening their bodies into a ribbon-like shape to catch the air. As they fall they slither in midair, swaying side to side, which keeps them stable and stretches the glide. They can sail surprisingly far this way to travel or escape danger.

In many turtles, crocodiles, and alligators, the temperature of the nest decides whether the eggs become male or female, not their genes. For American alligators, warmer nests tend to produce males and cooler ones females, with a mix in between. This means a changing climate can tilt whole populations toward one sex.

The largest family of salamanders has no lungs at all and breathes entirely through its moist skin and the lining of its mouth. Because they must stay damp to take in oxygen, these lungless salamanders live in cool, wet places like forest floors and streamsides. They make up a big share of all the salamander species on Earth.

The gharial is a crocodile relative from South Asia with an extremely long, thin snout lined with many interlocking needle-like teeth. That slender jaw can sweep sideways through water with little resistance, perfect for snapping up fish. Adult males grow a bulbous lump on the tip of the snout, called a ghara, that they use to make buzzing sounds and blow bubbles.

A frog's eardrums are the round patches you can see on the sides of its head, right behind the eyes, with no outer ear at all. In some frogs, sound also travels in through the lungs, and even the eyes can press down to protect the inner ear from a frog's own loud calls. This lets males pick out the call of their own species in a noisy chorus.

Snakes can't blink because they have no movable eyelids; instead each eye is covered by a clear, fused scale called a spectacle, or brille. This see-through cap protects the eye and is shed along with the rest of the skin, which is why a snake's eyes look cloudy and bluish just before it sheds. It is basically a built-in goggle that the snake replaces regularly.

Galápagos giant tortoises are among the longest-lived land animals, with some reaching well over 100 years. They can go a remarkably long time without food or water by storing it in their bodies and burning energy slowly. Sailors once exploited this by stacking the tortoises in ship holds as living, long-lasting food, which nearly wiped some island populations out.

The mudpuppy is a fully aquatic salamander that keeps showy, feathery external gills its whole life, sticking out behind its head like red plumes. The gills fluff out larger in still, warm, low-oxygen water and shrink smaller in cold, fast streams that already hold plenty of oxygen. Despite the spooky folk names people give it, the mudpuppy is harmless.

Spitting cobras can fire venom out of forward-facing holes in their fangs, aiming for an attacker's eyes from a distance. They tend to target movement around the face, and the venom can cause intense pain and even blindness if not rinsed away quickly. Spraying venom is a defense, while these snakes still bite to actually catch and subdue their prey.

The African egg-eating snake survives almost entirely on bird eggs many times wider than its own slim head. It unhinges its jaws and stretches its skin to swallow an egg whole, then bony spikes that poke down from its backbone saw through the shell inside its throat. The snake squeezes out the contents and neatly spits the crushed shell back up.

When a tadpole turns into a frog, far more changes than just growing legs and losing the tail. Its long, coiled, plant-digesting gut shortens into a much smaller meat-eating intestine, and it switches from breathing with gills to using lungs and skin. The tail isn't dropped off but is reabsorbed, its material recycled to help build the new adult body.

Sharks grow their teeth in conveyor-belt rows, so when a front tooth breaks or falls out, one from the row behind rotates forward to replace it within days. Over a lifetime a single shark can go through tens of thousands of teeth. That is why fossil shark teeth are so common to find on beaches.

Seahorses are fish, and in their world it is the father who gets pregnant. The female deposits her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly, where he fertilizes them, carries them, and eventually gives birth to dozens or hundreds of tiny seahorses. Seahorses also swim upright and grip seaweed with their curly tails.

Mudskippers are fish that spend a lot of time out of the water, hopping across mudflats on their muscular front fins. They breathe partly through their skin and the lining of their mouth and throat as long as those stay damp. Some even climb mangrove roots and dig burrows in the mud to shelter in.

A hammerhead shark's wide, flattened head spreads its eyes and sensory organs far apart, giving it nearly 360-degree vision and a better map of the electrical signals living things give off. This helps it find stingrays buried in the sand. Great hammerheads sometimes pin a ray to the seafloor with the side of their head before eating it.

When threatened, a pufferfish gulps water to balloon into a spiky ball several times its normal size, making it too big and prickly to swallow. Many puffers also carry tetrodotoxin, a poison far stronger than cyanide. In Japan, the puffer dish fugu is prepared only by specially licensed chefs trained to remove the toxic parts.

Megalodon was an enormous prehistoric shark, possibly around 50 feet or more in length, that hunted whales millions of years ago. We know it mainly from fossil teeth the size of a grown person's hand, because shark skeletons are made of cartilage and rarely fossilize. Despite some movies, it has been extinct for millions of years.

Fish breathe by pumping water over their gills, where blood flows in the opposite direction to the water in a clever setup called countercurrent exchange. Because the two flows run opposite ways, the blood can pull out far more oxygen than it could otherwise. This is why most fish suffocate in air even though air is full of oxygen, since their gills collapse and stick together.

The stonefish is the most venomous fish known, lying motionless and disguised as a rock or lump of coral on the seafloor. If stepped on, the sharp spines along its back inject venom that causes intense pain. Its camouflage is so good that the danger usually comes from people accidentally standing on one in shallow water.

The sawfish is actually a type of ray with a long flat snout lined with teeth-like spikes, which it swings sideways to slash and stun fish. That saw is also studded with sensors that detect the tiny electric fields of hidden prey. Sawfish are critically endangered, partly because their distinctive saws snag easily in fishing nets.

Bull sharks can swim far up rivers into freshwater, and they have been spotted hundreds of miles inland in rivers like the Mississippi and the Amazon. Their bodies can adjust how they handle salt so they survive in both ocean and river water. This habit means they sometimes turn up in surprisingly unexpected places far from the sea.

When thousands of fish wheel and flash as one, no leader is in charge; each fish simply watches its neighbors and matches their speed and direction. They sense the water movement of nearby fish through a row of pressure-detecting organs along their sides called the lateral line. Tight schooling confuses predators, who struggle to lock onto a single target in the swirling mass.

Antarctic icefish have clear, almost colorless blood because they are the only known vertebrates with no hemoglobin, the molecule that makes blood red and carries oxygen. They survive because cold water holds a lot of oxygen and the fish absorb it straight through their blood and skin. Many polar fish also make natural antifreeze proteins so their bodies do not freeze solid.

The thresher shark has an upper tail fin nearly as long as the rest of its body, and it uses it like a whip. Swimming into a school of fish, it snaps that huge tail forward so fast it stuns or kills several fish at once, then circles back to eat them. It is one of the few animals known to hunt by smacking its prey with its tail.

Shark skin feels smooth one way and like sandpaper the other because it is covered in tiny tooth-shaped scales called dermal denticles. These scales reduce drag and help sharks slip through the water quietly and efficiently. Engineers studied them to design faster swimsuits and even coatings for ships and airplanes.

Most trees are wired together underground by fungal threads called mycorrhizae, which fuse to the roots and act like an internet for the forest. Through this network, trees can trade sugar, water, and even chemical warning signals about pests. A single teaspoon of healthy forest soil can hold miles of these fungal threads.

When a plant bends toward a window, it's responding to a hormone called auxin that piles up on the shaded side of the stem. That side's cells stretch longer than the lit side, so the stem curves toward the light like a slow-motion lean. The plant isn't reaching for the sun on purpose, it's just growing unevenly on purpose.

Bamboo is technically a giant grass, not a tree, and some species can grow more than a meter in a single day. You could almost watch it move if you sat still long enough. It pulls this off by stretching out segments that were already pre-built inside the shoot, like an extending telescope.

Many seeds can stay alive but asleep for years, waiting for the exact right signal before sprouting. Some need fire's heat, some need to pass through an animal's gut, and some need a long cold winter so they don't sprout in autumn just before a freeze. A date palm seed roughly 2,000 years old, found near the Dead Sea, was successfully sprouted by scientists.

Each year a tree adds a pale ring in fast spring growth and a dark ring in slow summer growth, so counting the dark bands tells you its age. The rings also record the weather: a wet year leaves a fat ring, a drought leaves a thin one. Scientists can match ring patterns from ancient wood to build weather records thousands of years long.

A Venus flytrap actually counts before it snaps shut. Tiny trigger hairs inside the trap must be touched twice within about twenty seconds, which stops it wasting energy on raindrops or dust. Even more impressive, it keeps counting after closing to decide how much digestive juice to release for the size of the catch.

A grove of quaking aspen in Utah called Pando looks like thousands of separate trees, but they are all one organism sharing a single root system. Every trunk is a genetically identical clone, sprouting up from the same ancient roots. By that measure Pando is one of the heaviest and oldest living things on Earth.

Coast redwoods are the tallest living things on Earth, with some topping 100 meters, taller than a 30-story building. Getting water that high is hard, so the treetops drink straight from fog, soaking moisture in through their needles. Scientists have to climb them with ropes just to measure them.

Trees move water from roots to leaves through narrow straws called xylem, and there is no pump doing the work. Instead, water evaporating from the leaves pulls the whole column upward, with each water molecule clinging to the one below it. A separate set of pipes, the phloem, carries sugary food down from the leaves to the rest of the tree.

Leaves are actually orange and yellow all summer, but green chlorophyll is so bright it hides those colors. In autumn the tree stops making chlorophyll to save resources for winter, and the hidden pigments finally show through. The tree then seals off each leaf at the stem, letting it drop so it isn't a fragile water-loser in the cold.

A strange desert plant called welwitschia grows just two leaves its entire life, but never sheds them, so they keep growing for over a thousand years. Wind shreds those two leaves into ragged ribbons that look like a tangled pile. Some living welwitschia plants in the Namib Desert are estimated to be well over a thousand years old.

A tree gets taller only at the tips of its branches and roots, so a nail hammered into a trunk stays at the same height forever. The trunk gets fatter thanks to a thin living layer just under the bark called the cambium, which adds a fresh sleeve of wood every year. The old wood in the center is dead and acts as the tree's skeleton.

Plants need nitrogen to grow, but they can't use the nitrogen gas that makes up most of the air around them. Beans, clover, and peas solve this by housing special bacteria in lumps on their roots that pull nitrogen out of the air and turn it into plant food. Farmers plant these crops to naturally refill the soil's nitrogen for the next planting.

The resurrection plant can dry out into a brown lifeless-looking ball and survive that way for years. Add water and within hours it unfurls, greens up, and starts living again as if nothing happened. It pulls this off by replacing the water in its cells with a sugar that keeps the cell parts from collapsing while dry.

When a leaf gets chewed, many plants fight back by flooding the leaf with bitter or toxic chemicals to make themselves taste awful. Some, like acacia trees, also release a gas that drifts to nearby trees as a warning, prompting neighbors to ramp up their own defenses before the pest even arrives. So a herd grazing one tree can find the next ones suddenly unappetizing.

Mushrooms look like they belong with plants, but fungi are actually a separate kingdom of life, closer to animals than to plants in some ways. They have no chlorophyll and can't make food from sunlight, so instead they digest dead matter or partner with tree roots. The mushroom you see is just the fruit; most of the fungus is a hidden web of threads in the soil.

A coconut is one giant seed built to sail. Its thick fibrous husk traps air so it floats, and the hard shell keeps seawater out while the milk inside feeds the sprout. Coconuts can drift across oceans for weeks and still wash up on a new beach ready to grow, which is how they colonized islands worldwide.

Some plants never touch the ground at all, living perched on tree branches high in the canopy to grab more light. These air plants, like many orchids and bromeliads, soak up rain and dust through their leaves instead of roots in soil. They aren't parasites, they just use the tree as a sunny apartment.

When a seed wakes up, the very first thing to emerge is a root that pushes downward, no matter which way the seed is lying. The seed senses gravity, so the root always heads down and the shoot always heads up. Inside the seed is a packed lunch of starch that feeds the baby plant until its first leaves can start making food.

Some pine and eucalyptus trees lock their seeds inside cones or pods sealed shut with resin, opening them only when a wildfire's heat melts the seal. This way the seeds drop onto freshly cleared, ash-fertilized ground with no competition. For these plants a forest fire isn't a disaster, it's the starting gun for the next generation.

The sensitive plant folds its leaves shut within seconds of being touched, drooping as if startled. It does this by rapidly dumping water out of cells at the base of each leaf, so they go limp like a deflating air mattress. The trick may scare off insects or make the plant look less tasty, and the leaves slowly puff back open afterward.

A banyan tree drops roots down from its branches that thicken into new trunks when they reach the ground. Over many years one tree can spread into what looks like a small forest, with hundreds of trunks holding up a single enormous canopy. The largest banyans can shade an area big enough to fit thousands of people underneath.

Great Basin bristlecone pines are among the oldest individual living things on Earth, with some over 4,800 years old, older than the pyramids of Giza when they were finished. They survive by growing painfully slowly in harsh, dry mountain conditions, which makes their wood dense and rot-resistant. Often most of the tree is dead, kept alive by just a thin strip of living bark.

Plants cool themselves much the way you do when you sweat. Water evaporating from leaf pores carries heat away, which is why a forest feels cooler than a parking lot on a hot day. A single large tree can release hundreds of liters of water into the air on a warm day through this process.

The titan arum, or corpse flower, produces one of the largest flowering structures in the world and smells like rotting meat when it blooms. The stink is a clever trick to attract flies and beetles that normally lay eggs on dead animals, tricking them into carrying pollen instead. It may wait years between blooms, and each bloom lasts only a day or two.

Gardeners can join a branch from one plant onto the trunk of another, and if the cuts line up just right, the two fuse and grow as one. This is how a single apple tree can be made to grow several different varieties of apple at once. Almost every apple in the store comes from a grafted tree, because seeds from a tasty apple rarely grow into a tree with the same fruit.

Moss is one of the oldest types of land plant and it has no real roots, no flowers, and no internal plumbing to move water around. Instead it soaks up moisture directly through its tiny leaves like a sponge, which is why moss tends to grow in damp, shady spots. It reproduces with dust-like spores rather than seeds, the same way its ancestors did hundreds of millions of years ago.

Young sunflowers swing their faces to follow the sun across the sky each day, then turn back east overnight to be ready for sunrise. This tracking is driven by one side of the stem growing faster than the other through the day. Once a sunflower matures it stops dancing and settles facing east, which warms its blooms earlier and draws in more pollinating bees.

Lichen isn't a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and an alga living as one. The alga makes food from sunlight while the fungus provides shelter and grabs water and minerals, so together they survive on bare rock where neither could live alone. Lichens grow incredibly slowly, sometimes less than a millimeter a year, so a large patch can be centuries old.

The largest living organism known on Earth isn't a whale or a tree, it's a honey fungus growing in the Blue Mountains of Oregon. Most of it lives underground as a vast web of root-like threads spreading across thousands of acres, and it's thought to be thousands of years old. The mushrooms you might see on the surface are just tiny temporary fruiting bodies of this enormous hidden giant.

Most of a fungus is invisible, living as a tangle of microscopic threads called mycelium that spreads through soil, wood, or leaves. A mushroom is just the fruiting part a fungus pushes up to release spores, like an apple is to a tree. A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain miles of these fine fungal threads laid end to end.

Billions of years ago, tiny bacteria called cyanobacteria learned to use sunlight to make food and released oxygen as waste. Over a vast stretch of time they flooded Earth's atmosphere with oxygen, an event so huge it's called the Great Oxidation. Almost every breath you take traces back to the work these microbes started long before there were any plants or animals.

Slime molds are strange blobs that aren't plants, animals, or fungi, yet they can solve mazes to reach food despite having no brain at all. In one famous experiment, a slime mold grew tubes connecting food sources in a pattern remarkably similar to a real city's rail network. It seems to 'remember' where it has already been by leaving a slimy trail it avoids re-crossing.

Fungi reproduce by releasing spores, single cells so tiny and light they float on the breeze for great distances. A single large mushroom can release billions of spores, and the air all around you almost always carries some. Some fungi fling their spores with surprising force, launching them at accelerations far greater than a rocket leaving the ground.

Dozens of mushroom species glow softly in the dark with a greenish light, a phenomenon people once called foxfire when they spotted it on rotting logs in the forest. The glow comes from a chemical reaction similar to the one fireflies use. Scientists think the light may attract insects that then help spread the fungus's spores around.

A fungus called Ophiocordyceps infects certain ants and effectively hijacks their behavior, driving the doomed insect to climb up and clamp onto a leaf in just the right spot. The fungus then kills the ant and sprouts a stalk from its head to rain spores down on the colony below. This real-life 'zombie' fungus inspired the monsters in popular video games and shows.

Deep on the ocean floor, where sunlight never reaches and water gushes out of vents hot enough to melt lead, bacteria thrive by eating chemicals from the Earth instead of using sunlight. Entire communities of giant tube worms, crabs, and clams depend on these microbes for food. Their discovery showed that life can flourish in places once thought completely impossible.

Plants need nitrogen to grow, but they can't grab it from the air directly even though air is mostly nitrogen. Special bacteria living in lumps on the roots of beans, peas, and clover do it for them, pulling nitrogen from the air and turning it into a form the plant can use. This natural fertilizer factory is why farmers often rotate these crops to refresh tired soil.

Fungi are among the few living things that can break down lignin, the tough material that makes wood hard and stiff. Without them, dead trees and fallen leaves would pile up endlessly instead of rotting back into soil. By recycling dead matter, fungi free up nutrients so new plants can grow, quietly keeping forests alive.

Fungi are not plants, and surprisingly they're more closely related to animals than to anything green. Like us, they can't make their own food and have to absorb nutrients from their surroundings. They even build their cell walls from chitin, the same tough material found in the shells of crabs and the bodies of insects.

A bacterium nicknamed Conan the Bacterium can shrug off doses of radiation that would be thousands of times lethal to a human. It survives by holding multiple copies of its genetic code and rapidly stitching its DNA back together after the blast shatters it. Scientists are studying it for ideas about repairing damage and protecting astronauts on long space journeys.

Your mouth is home to hundreds of different kinds of bacteria, and the sticky film on your teeth in the morning is a crowded city of them called a biofilm. These bacteria feed on leftover sugars and produce acids that can wear holes in your teeth. Brushing and flossing isn't just about freshness, it's about breaking up that microbial city before it does damage.

Truffles are fungi that grow entirely underground near tree roots and never poke up above the surface. Because they can't release spores into the air, they instead produce a powerful smell that lures animals to dig them up and spread the spores elsewhere. That same intoxicating aroma makes certain truffles one of the most expensive foods in the world, sniffed out by trained dogs and pigs.

The good bacteria in your gut especially love fiber, the part of fruits, beans, and whole grains that your own body can't digest. When they ferment that fiber, they release helpful compounds that nourish the cells lining your intestine. Feeding these microbes well is one reason a diet rich in plants tends to keep your digestion happy.

Many beloved foods like yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut, and kimchi are made by letting helpful bacteria feast on the ingredients. As the bacteria eat sugars, they produce acids that give these foods their tangy taste and keep harmful germs from spoiling them. People have used this microbe-powered trick to preserve food for thousands of years, long before refrigerators existed.

Mycorrhizal fungi act a little like underground traders, and experiments show they can drive a kind of bargain with plants. Fungi tend to deliver more nutrients to plant roots that pay them more sugar in return, and pull back from stingy partners. This back-and-forth, with no brains involved, keeps both sides cooperating instead of cheating.

Some bacteria can't live where there's oxygen and instead thrive in sealed, airless places like improperly canned food. One of them, Clostridium botulinum, produces one of the most powerful natural poisons known. In tiny, purified doses that same toxin is used as the wrinkle-smoothing treatment Botox, showing how the line between deadly and useful can be very thin.

When conditions get harsh, some bacteria seal themselves inside an incredibly tough protective shell called an endospore and basically switch off. In this state they can endure boiling, drying, and starvation for astonishingly long times. Scientists have reported reviving bacterial spores recovered from extremely old material, hinting these capsules can outlast almost anything until good times return.

Athlete's foot and ringworm are caused by fungi that feed on keratin, the protein in your skin, hair, and nails. Despite its name, ringworm isn't a worm at all, just a fungus that often spreads in a circular ring-shaped rash. These fungi love warm, damp places, which is why locker rooms and sweaty shoes are their favorite hangouts.

Certain fungi and bacteria can break down pollutants, and scientists put them to work cleaning up messes in a process called bioremediation. Some microbes munch through spilled oil, while certain fungi can digest harmful chemicals and even help rot away stubborn waste. There are even mushrooms being tested for their ability to break down plastics and toxins humans struggle to dispose of.

Bacteria are so small that millions could fit on the head of a pin, and nobody knew they existed until microscopes got good enough to see them. In the 1670s a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own tiny lenses and became the first person to spy these wriggling creatures, which he called 'animalcules.' He found them in pond water, rain, and even the scrapings from his own teeth.

Brewer's yeast, the same fungus that makes bread and beer, is one of the most important organisms in all of biology research. Because its cells work in many of the same basic ways ours do and it grows quickly in the lab, scientists use it to study how living cells function and divide. A surprising number of its genes have close matches in humans, so studying yeast has helped uncover clues about diseases including cancer.

keywords: metal that melts in your hand
facts.answer: Gallium is a soft, silvery metal with a melting point of about 30 degrees Celsius, so a chunk of it will turn to liquid in the warmth of your palm. People sometimes cast it into spoons that quietly dissolve into a puddle when stirred into a hot drink. It is harmless to touch but stains your skin a bit, and it expands when it freezes, like water does.

Helium was spotted on the Sun before anyone found it on Earth. In 1868, astronomers studying sunlight during a solar eclipse saw a yellow line in the spectrum that matched no known element, so they named it after Helios, the Greek sun god. It took another 27 years before helium was finally isolated from a mineral here on the ground.

Francium is so rare and so radioactive that scientists estimate there is only a tiny amount of it in the entire Earth's crust at any moment. It decays away almost as fast as it forms, with its most stable form lasting only about 22 minutes. Because of this, nobody has ever collected enough francium to see a visible chunk of it.

Diamond, the hardest natural material, and graphite, the soft stuff in pencils, are both made of nothing but carbon atoms. The wild difference comes entirely from how the atoms are arranged: diamond locks them into a rigid 3D grid, while graphite stacks them in slippery flat sheets. Carbon can also form hollow soccer-ball molecules and one-atom-thick sheets called graphene.

Technetium was the first element created by humans in a lab rather than found in nature, made in 1937. Its name even comes from the Greek word for 'artificial'. It has no stable form at all, and it filled a gap in the periodic table that had puzzled chemists for years.

Copper surfaces naturally kill many bacteria and viruses that land on them, often within hours, which is why some hospitals fit copper door handles and railings. The metal releases ions that punch holes in microbe cell membranes. Ancient peoples noticed water stored in copper vessels stayed fresher, long before anyone understood why.

Neon glows a bright orange-red when electricity passes through it, and that is the only true color real neon gas makes. All the other colors in 'neon' signs actually come from different gases or colored tubes. Neon is a noble gas, meaning it almost never reacts with anything else.

Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by an alchemist who boiled down large amounts of urine hoping to make gold and instead got a waxy substance that glowed in the dark. White phosphorus is so reactive it can burst into flame in air, and its eerie green glow is where the word 'phosphorescent' comes from. Your own body needs phosphorus for bones, teeth, and DNA.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any pure metal, staying solid until well above 3400 degrees Celsius. That is why old incandescent light bulbs use thin tungsten wire that can glow white-hot without melting. Its name means 'heavy stone' in Swedish, and it is one of the densest metals around.

Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth, and scientists believe less than a teaspoon's worth exists in the entire planet's crust at any one time. It is so radioactive that a visible piece would instantly vaporize itself with its own heat. Almost everything we know about it comes from studying tiny lab-made amounts.

Pure sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, fizzing, skating across the surface, and sometimes bursting into flame. Because it grabs moisture from the air, it is stored under oil to keep it safe. Strangely, this dangerous metal combines with poisonous chlorine gas to make ordinary, edible table salt.

Gold is one of the least reactive metals, which is why coins and jewelry made of it thousands of years ago still gleam without rust or tarnish. It is also incredibly malleable: a single gram can be hammered into a sheet thin enough to cover much of a small table. Most of the gold on Earth likely arrived from ancient meteorite impacts and stellar collisions.

Solid iodine skips the liquid stage and turns straight into a striking purple vapor when gently warmed, a process called sublimation. Your thyroid gland needs small amounts of iodine to work properly, which is why it is added to table salt in many countries. The element's name comes from the Greek word for violet.

Lithium is the lightest of all metals and is so low in density that it actually floats on water, though it reacts with the water at the same time. It powers the rechargeable batteries in phones, laptops, and electric cars by shuttling tiny ions back and forth. In nature it is never found as the pure metal because it is too eager to react.

Radon is an invisible, odorless radioactive gas that seeps up from certain rocks and soil and can collect in basements. Even though it is a noble gas that barely reacts chemically, it is dangerous because it gives off radiation as it decays. Many homes are tested for it, and simple ventilation can keep levels safe.

Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that is poisonous to breathe, yet tiny amounts of it keep swimming pools and drinking water free of harmful germs. It was the first chemical weapon used in World War I. Combined with sodium, this deadly gas becomes the harmless salt sprinkled on your fries.

Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe, far more than oxygen, yet it is so unreactive that it mostly passes straight in and out of your lungs. Cooled into a liquid, it is cold enough to freeze a flower solid in seconds and shatter it like glass. Plants depend on special bacteria to convert nitrogen from the air into a form they can actually use.

Cesium is so reactive it can ignite on contact with air or water, but its steady vibrations are also used to define exactly how long one second is. The world's most precise atomic clocks count the oscillations of cesium atoms and would lose less than a second over millions of years. It is also one of the softest metals, easily cut with a knife.

Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen, and it is the main ingredient in ordinary sand and quartz. Purified into near-perfect crystals, it becomes the brain material for nearly every computer chip and solar cell on the planet. An entire region of California is nicknamed Silicon Valley because of it.

Antimony has been used since ancient times, and a compound of it was the dark kohl that Egyptians painted around their eyes thousands of years ago. As a metalloid, it sits on the fence between metals and nonmetals in its behavior. Today it shows up in flame-retardant materials and in some battery and alloy mixtures.

Potassium burns with a striking lilac-purple flame, a trick chemists use to identify it. Like sodium, it is a soft metal that reacts vigorously with water. You also carry plenty of potassium in your body, where it helps nerves fire and muscles move, and foods like bananas are a tasty source of it.

Platinum is rarer than gold and so dense that a cube the size of a sugar cube weighs more than you might expect. It works as a catalyst, speeding up chemical reactions without being used up, which is why it sits inside car exhaust systems cleaning up harmful gases. It also barely corrodes, making it prized for fine jewelry and lab equipment.

Argon is the third most plentiful gas in the air after nitrogen and oxygen, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'lazy' because it almost never reacts with anything.
